summary: This RFC specifies the Password Generator service, which returns six random eight-character words with reasonable pronounceability, using a multi-level algorithm. Hosts that choose to offer such a service are expected to follow it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 972 defines a service that returns a short list of pronounceable random words for a user to choose as a password. It describes both a TCP connection and a UDP request and reply.

subtitle: A network service that offers pronounceable passwords for users to choose from.

tldr.problem: Random passwords can be difficult to remember, while user-selected words can be too easy to guess.
tldr.mechanism: A PWDGEN server returns six randomly generated, eight-character words designed to have a reasonable level of pronounceability.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines TCP and UDP service forms on port 129 and emphasizes that password uniqueness depends on a sufficiently random seed.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 972's status as Unknown. The RFC specifies a standard for ARPA Internet hosts that choose to implement the PWDGEN service.

sections.title: Passwords That Are Easier to Remember
sections.content:
The RFC says ordinary user-selected passwords may be easy to guess. Random passwords can be difficult to remember when they cannot be pronounced, and a short-cycle pseudo-random generator can reduce uniqueness.

PWDGEN offers a set of candidate words for a user to choose from, with an option to request another set. The RFC says that the uniqueness of the words depends strongly on the randomness of the initial seed.
sections.plainLanguage: The service generates a list so users can choose a password instead of making one up. Its results depend on how well the system chooses its starting seed.

sections.title: The PWDGEN Response
sections.content:
The service returns six random words, each eight characters long, separated by carriage-return and line-feed sequences. The RFC describes the words as having a reasonable level of pronounceability and refers system administrators to a FORTRAN-77 algorithm implementation.

It recommends a shared system-wide seed that is updated after each access. Seeds based on a time-of-day clock are described as unacceptable, and seed values larger than 32 bits are recommended for best performance.
sections.plainLanguage: A request produces six candidate words, separated onto lines. A strong, changing seed helps reduce repeated or predictable results.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Service Options
sections.content:
For TCP, a server listens on port 129. After a client connects, the server sends the six words and closes the connection; the RFC defines no dialogue.

For UDP, a server listens for datagrams on port 129 and sends the six words in a reply datagram. Both forms return the same candidate list.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can request passwords through either TCP or UDP. In both cases the server returns the list and does not conduct a back-and-forth conversation.
